intro: Soccer left London after 1863. FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904. Basketball left a Springfield YMCA gym after 1891. The Hall of Fame stayed in that city. Illinois still uses IHSA rules for school series.

Martial-arts rooms sit next door: a wrestling mat, a boxing ring, a fencing strip. Kano shaped judo in Japan and Olympic judo debuted in Tokyo in 1964. That full history is The Measured Step. Both books refuse technique.
bigQuestion: How do games travel, and why does martial-arts history need its own book?

title: Many Games, One Book

chapters.title: Games That Travel
chapters.bigQuestion: How did soccer and basketball move from one town to many countries?

story.title: A Ball With No Writing
story.kicker: A worn ball in a closet has no team logo, only the marks of many hands.
paragraphs: The closet ball is brown and scuffed. No league name is printed on it. Still, children in two countries would know a round ball and a rectangle of grass.
Soccer left London after 1863 because ships, schools, and clubs carried the written rules. Basketball left Springfield after 1891 because YMCA teachers carried the gym game.
A game travels when people copy the room and the words. It does not travel by magic. The page and the place both move. The names stay on the page.
This chapter names two trips: soccer across oceans, and basketball out of one Massachusetts gym into other gyms. The names stay on the page.
story.think: What would you pack for a game to travel: a ball, a rule book, or both?

lessons.title: Rules on Paper Can Sail
lessons.mainIdea: After 1863, sailors, students, and clubs carried association football far from London.
reading: Once the Football Association wrote rules in 1863, the kicking game could be taught from a page. People copied the page in new ports.
British sailors and students played abroad. Local clubs formed. The game was no longer only a London club sport.

words.d: a group that meets to play and that can join a written code

lessons.mainIdea: FIFA, founded in 1904 in Paris, is a world office for association football.
reading: *FIFA* is the world body for soccer. It was founded in Paris in 1904. It came after the Football Association, not before.
FIFA does not replace IFAB's Laws of the Game. It organizes world competitions among national associations.

lessons.title: YMCA Teachers Carried the Gym Game
lessons.mainIdea: YMCA teachers took basketball from Springfield to other gyms in the 1890s.
reading: Naismith taught at a YMCA training school. Students who left Springfield took the new game with them to other YMCA gyms.
The peach baskets became hoops. The idea that traveled first was an indoor gym game with a raised goal.

lessons.title: A Hall of Fame Stayed in Springfield
lessons.mainIdea: The Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame is in Springfield, Massachusetts, where the game began.
reading: Springfield still marks the invention. The Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame stands in that city.
The hall is a museum. It is not the only place basketball is played. It keeps the origin story on purpose.

lessons.title: Copy the Room and the Words
lessons.mainIdea: A game travels when people copy both the place it needs and the words that run it.
reading: Soccer needed a pitch and the Laws. Basketball needed a gym and a raised goal. Copying only the ball is not enough.
If a town has a ball but no agreed words, two groups will argue about the start. Traveling games bring their rule books with them.

words.d: when a game is copied in a new town with its room and its words

lessons.title: Illinois Plays Games Born Elsewhere
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois school fields host soccer and basketball, games that began in other places.
reading: An Illinois gym can host basketball even though the game began in Massachusetts in 1891. An Illinois pitch can host soccer even though the FA began in London in 1863.
The IHSA writes the school rules for those sports here. The birthplace stays in the history. The local handbook runs the state series.

chapters.title: The Measured Step Lives Next Door
chapters.bigQuestion: How is a martial-arts school different from a ball field, and where is that history taught?

story.title: A Jacket Beside a Ball Bag
story.kicker: A folded white jacket hangs in a hallway next to a bag of baseballs.
paragraphs: The hallway has two hooks. On one hook hangs a folded white jacket and a belt. On the other hangs a bag of balls. Both belong to after-school groups.
The jacket is a gi, school clothes for some martial-arts classes. The balls belong to diamond and gym games. They share a building. They do not share a rule book.
Ms. Ortiz says Sports History will not teach a throw or a strike. That history has its own book. The book is called The Measured Step.
Today we only learn names of rooms: mat, ring, and strip, and why those rooms are not a soccer pitch. The names stay on the page.
story.think: Why might two after-school groups in one hall still need two books?

lessons.title: A Mat Is Not a Pitch
lessons.mainIdea: School wrestling uses a mat. Soccer uses a pitch. They are different rooms.
reading: School wrestling in Illinois is practiced on a padded *mat*. The IHSA held its first boys wrestling state meet in 1937.
A soccer pitch is grass or turf with goals. A wrestling mat is not a pitch. Calling both the gym floor hides the difference.

words.d: the padded floor used for school wrestling

lessons.title: A Ring and a Strip
lessons.mainIdea: Boxing uses a roped square called a ring. Fencing uses a long narrow strip.
reading: A boxing *ring* is a square with ropes. It is not a circle, even though it is called a ring. Early IHSA rules kept boxing out of Illinois school sport.
Fencing is played on a long narrow *strip*, also called a piste. That thin floor is the room. It is not a soccer pitch.

lessons.title: A Jacket and a Belt
lessons.mainIdea: A gi and a belt are school clothes and class marks, not weapons.
reading: Some martial-arts schools use a jacket called a *gi* and a colored *belt*. The belt marks the class, like a grade on a door.
A wrestling singlet is different school clothing. Clothes tell you which room you are in. They do not teach a hit.

lessons.title: Judo Has a Writer
lessons.mainIdea: Jigoro Kano shaped judo as a school with a code in Japan in the late 1800s.
reading: Jigoro *Kano* taught in Japan in the late 1800s. He shaped *judo* as a school sport with ranks and written aims, not as a battlefield drill.
Judo later became an Olympic sport in Tokyo in 1964. Those facts belong in The Measured Step. This book only names them so the two shelves stay clear.

It does not teach a strike, choke, or throw. This Sports History course does not teach those either. Both books refuse technique.

lessons.title: Rituals Are Described, Not Led
lessons.mainIdea: Bowing in a martial-arts school is explained as a school sign, not practiced in this lesson.
reading: Some martial-arts schools bow when they enter a hall. In this course we *describe* that custom. We do not practice it as a class ritual.
The same rule holds for sitting quietly or handling a ritual object. Explain the sign. Do not lead it. Public-school history stays on that line.

words.d: to tell what a custom is without asking students to do it
